title: Loss Aversion

scenes.text: Losing ₹500 hurts more than finding ₹500 feels *good*.
scenes.vo: Losing 500 rupees hurts way more than finding 500 rupees feels good. Here's why.

scenes.text:
Losses feel about
*2×* stronger than gains
scenes.vo: Kahneman and Tversky found that losses feel roughly twice as powerful as gains of the same size.

scenes.text:
Heads: win ₹1,000
Tails: lose ₹1,000
Would you play?
scenes.vo: Would you take a coin flip to win or lose a thousand rupees? Most people say no.

scenes.text:
Most people want a win of
*~₹2,000* before they'll bet
scenes.vo: Most people only take the bet when the possible win is around double the possible loss.
This is loss aversion. Your brain guards what you have more fiercely than it chases what you could get.

scenes.text:
Free trials. “Last chance.”
Holding losing stocks.
scenes.vo: It's why free trials work, since cancelling feels like losing something. And why 'last chance' hits harder than 'great deal'.

scenes.text: Flip the frame: what would I *gain* by letting go?
scenes.vo: Before your next decision, flip the frame. Ask: what would I gain by letting go?

scenes.text:
Follow *@inquisitive_bytes*
for a daily byte of behaviour science
scenes.vo: Follow Inquisitive Bytes for a daily byte of behaviour science.

caption:
Your brain is a terrible accountant: a loss weighs roughly twice as much as an equal gain. 📉

What's something you held onto just because letting go felt like losing? 👇
source: Kahneman, D. & Tversky, A. (1979). Prospect Theory. Econometrica, 47(2); Tversky & Kahneman (1992), Journal of Risk and Uncertainty.
